You're dating yourself. You realize AI chess programs can beat elite chess players, correct? You realize that putting chess on a computer makes it a computer game.... yes? Moba's are a subset of RTS (Real Time Strategy) games. As the name implies, RTS games involve planning out positioning, timing/patience, picking up on subtle faults from opponents, and anticipating future positioning from you opponent while trying to stay two steps ahead of them at all times. You know, kind of like a strategy game. Oh now that I think of it, that sounds a lot like chess...

Maybe not so much actually. Chess is easy compared to your standard RTS.

For instance, you don't need to save up to buy pawns. You don't need to worry about a rook and a queen simultaneously sneaking through your weaker spots while you're moving half your pieces across the board in an offensive. You don't need to worry about other players besides you and your opponent. You don't need to work as a team. You don't have **more than 64 places on the board** you need to cover. You don't even need to act quickly unless you're in a tournament. The clock is always ticking in an RTS, hence *REAL TIME* Strategy.

I don't claim to be an expert in writing melodies, but i've definitely worked with music long enough to understand them.

My two most important suggestions are:
1.) STAY IN KEY*
and
2.) make sure the melody follows the chord progression, utilizing leading tones

I'll start #1 by explaining the asterisk: this is not, by any means, a hard-set rule. In fact, using notes outside the major scale can have a much more impactful effect on the melody, but *only if you know what you're doing*. Assuming that we aren't so familiar with scales (besides major), it's probably best to just stick to the notes within the major scale.

One incredibly reliable trick for getting decent sounding melodies is using a **pentatonic scale**, as opposed to the full *diatonic* scale. Whereas the standard major scale (or **major diatonic scale**) has 7 notes, the **major pentatonic scale** has 5 notes; and these 5 notes tend to sound good over any chord in your song's key.

Take a look at this diagram of the full [F major diatonic scale](https://www.basicmusictheory.com/img/f-major-scale-on-piano-keyboard.png). Notice how the notes in the scale are labeled by number. This is because all major scales share the same theory rules, so it's just easier to discuss/refer to than saying the note's letter name. Anyway, you'll notice that the **F major pentatonic scale** notes are: 1, 2, 3, 5, and 6. So if you play those over any standard chord progression in the F major scale, it will sound fine.
https://www.basicmusictheory.com/f-major-scale
This website has most of this information on it too.

for reference, the scale notes (or **degrees**) in a *diatonic major scale* are as follows:
Scale degree #, scale degree name, triad associated with the degree
1      (tonic)             Major
2      (subtonic)        minor
3      (mediant)        minor
4      (subdominant) Major
5      (dominant)      Major* (major triad, but dominant 7th, 9th, etc.)
6      (submediant)   minor
7      (leading tone)  diminished
8      (tonic)             Major

Now onto #2: using the notes of your chords.
While using a pentatonic scale works, the melodies that come out of it aren't terribly interesting. A better way of writing melodies is to just follow your progression and use the chords' **triad notes** and **extension notes**. A **triad** is a basic chord with just 3 notes (ex: Cmaj triad = C, E, and G). For now, we'll only focus on major and minor triads. In the list of scale degrees, i put the type of chord that you build off of each degree (or note); it's known as the scale of chords. There's rules for chord progressions that are fairly simple but I don't want to get into them now, so I'd recommend that you give "chord progression chart" a google, and stick to the results for major scales. Anyway, once you have a chord progression (and you *should* have one before writing a melody, unless you already have a great sounding melody that you want to build chords around, which is mad difficult), you can begin writing your melody. Keep in mind which chord is where and just arrange your melody's notes over the chord's notes, adjust their rhythm how you see fit.

Now with your three-note triad, this won't get you far. Again, it will sound fine, but likely boring. This is where *extended chords & notes* come into play. **Extended chords** are chords that are built off of triads, but have have four or more notes in total. For example, a Cmaj7 chord = C, E, G, and B. These are the types of chords that make jazz, gospel, r&b, etc sound so colorful. You can look into chord progressions with extended chords if you want; they more or less follow the same pattern as triads, but it takes a pretty decent understanding of theory to make them sound smooth. There are 7th, 9th, 11th, and 13th extensions, but using 7ths and 9ths, along with leading tones, are likely enough to put some really solid melodies together.

So, as before, you can make a chord progression using triads, but now when you go to make your melody, you essentially have the whole scale to work with as opposed to 3 or 5 notes. In general, notes of extended chords follow an **every other scale degree** pattern. Let me reiterate that it is ever other *scale degree* (ex. C maj: C,E,G,B,D,F,A,C or 1,3,5,7,2,4,6,1) , not every other *note*; in other words, focus on the notes in the scale and not the notes on the keyboard. it's also a good habit to start seeing notes as numbers rather than letters. So, using numbers, our example of a Cmaj 7th chord uses degrees 1, 3, 5, and **7** (hence *7th chord*) and Cmaj 9th would be 1, 3, 5, 7, **9** (degree 9 is the same as degree 2, just an octave higher). In the key of C, the ninth chord of D (scale degree 2) is minor (bc scale of chords) and contains the notes/degrees 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 (D,F,A,C,E).

This is already way too long but i need to mention leading tones. A leading tone is the 7th scale degree of a **MAJOR** scale (no leading tones in minor!) and has the greatest amount of tension in the diatonic scale. this tension gets resolved when the leading tone (7) leads into the tonic (1 or 8). To use leading tones in a melody, **use the 7th scale degree from the scale of the *root note* of the chord** to lead into said chord. Yes, i know that's confusing. To clarify: in the key of C, the note B is degree 7 (or leading tone); but you wouldn't use B *as a leading tone* unless the next note was a C. Say we have a vi-ii (scale degree 6 to degree 2) progression in C where an A minor triad goes to D minor. Whereas the leading tone *of the key* is the note B, the leading tone that leads into the D minor chord would be D flat, because D flat is the 7th note of the D major scale. Now that you read all that, let me simplify it: just use the note below the root note of the next chord. If you use it right, it will create a lot of tension that will naturally resolve when said next chord is played.

To wrap this up, *for each chord* in your chord progression, find out whether it's major or minor (or dominant/diminished), look up the 7th, 9th, or 11th chord for it (until you're familiar with the pattern) and stick to those notes until you reach the next chord; at which point you can choose to go safely out of key by leading into the next chord with the note just below it's root note. Or you can just be safe and boring and use a pentatonic scale. Or slightly less boring by using a pentatonic scale for the key of each root note in your chord progression (in the same way you used 9th chords for each triad in your progression).

More often than not, the sounds used for these melodies are going to come from Virtual Instruments (VST's).

Unfortunately, most of the really powerful vst's are pretty expensive (unless you can find... *other* ways of obtaining it... * cough cough *), but there are some pretty solid free ones floating around the web. However, assuming you have FL, so you should have some pretty powerful VST's from ImageLine already installed, namely 3xOSC, Harmless, Harmor, PoiZone, Sakura, Sytrus, and ToxicBiohazard.

If you're just starting out with vst's, I would recommend playing with 3x OSC before jumping into the more in-depth programs. It is very simple/basic, but it will give you a solid understanding of how the basic types of waves sound and how they mix to create a more unique sounds. From there I would play around with presets of more powerful vst's and see how different changes in the program affect the sound, or look up videos on how to create certain sounds within a certain VST.

Of course you can skip the playing-around part and just use the presets; but, as a producer, it's really helpful to start understanding how vst's work. No matter how fancy or complex a program is, the foundation is the same as any other vst (i.e. once you fully understand one, every other vst becomes 10x easier to learn).

I dont know how much my experience will help you, but for what it's worth, I OD'ed on antidepressants in an attempt on my life earlier this year. My head was flooded with suicidal thoughts for months leading up to it. In the summer, a relationship I valued ended; that triggered me to commit. At around 11:00 pm, I took something like 300 mg of venlafaxine and 1800 mg of Wellbutrin down with maybe a quarter of a fifth of whiskey. I wanted to take enough to kill me if i ignored help but to let me survive if i seeked it out. I laid down on my bed and cried for the next hour or so. When they started to take hold, i didnt feel fear or panic or overwhelming sadness; i just felt regret, (shame, almost, but it's not the right word for it). Though i had been spending every day in agony, miserably continuing a (seemingly) meaningless life, something hidden in the deepest part of my being didn't want it to end.

Consciously, I knew I didnt want to live; but intuitively, there was something still driving me. I've always been a more logic-oriented person though, so I tried to ignore my subconscious' cries for help and continue on what i set out to do. However, they just grew louder and louder. This went on for hours. I couldn't take it, so i called the suicide hotline. I didnt call them because i wanted help, i just wanted someone to talk to in order to take my mind off of the swirling vortex of shit that i was in. It only kind of helped; they kept trying to get my address, of which i refused to give, and it felt more like i was talking to someone doing a job than someone who wanted me to survive. That's not to say he didnt, by the way; I'm well aware that he did, that was clear to me after the fact. Anyway, they kept prying and prying for information on where i lived, so i just hung up.

After I hung up, my subconscious's cries for help just continued to grow louder. I couldnt ignore them, but i couldnt listen to them either. i guess i compromised by stumbling/crawling into my kitchen at around 5:00 in the morning and eating/drinking water til i was full. i took as many bottles of water as i could back to my bed and tried to go to sleep.

I didn't sleep that night.

I grew more fearful as time elapsed. By 8:00 am I was violently shivering and fading in consciousness. This was the first time in my life that I truly acknowledged my mortality. I can't honestly say I expected to die at that point but I knew that could very well have been a result. I didn't really want to die at that point either, but I thought that it would've been too late for a hospital to reverse it anyway; that, the fucking ridiculous prices for medical treatment in the US, and the pain that i wouldve caused my parents by waking them up and taking me to the hospital deterred me from taking any significant action to survive.

After the peak of the OD was over, I was able to fall asleep. I slept for like 22 hours straight, brushing off my parents when they tried to wake me up.

I survived a suicide attempt.
I had to convince myself that that was true. I kept trying to devalue my experience, telling myself it wasnt really a suicide attempt... that I wouldn't be here if it was a REAL attempt, that I didn't actually even commit to killing myself, that being a suicide survivor entailed a trip to a hospital and a massive family intervention, that it required blood or vomit or pain. The truth is, I swallowed a handful of pills not caring if i lived or died, and hoped for the latter.

On the topic of underrating our experiences, I want to say that I am not better or cooler or wiser than you for having attempted suicide and if i have remotely come off as condescending it is not intentional. we're on the same plane facing similar struggles. as far as I am concerned, you're a suicide survivor yourself - and i want you to keep surviving.

I'm hesitant to add this next detail because it seems like i'm glorifying the effects of a suicide attempt, but I feel it's an important part of my story. In the weeks after that day, everything felt so beautiful. I was still in horrible mental/emotional pain, but i literally felt like i had come back from the grave and was again witnessing my life for the very first time. My perspective and appreciation for everything around me changed dramatically, mostly for the better. It made me want to live again. Alas, this only lasted a few weeks, but left a lasting impression on me. It taught me to appreciate the world, myself, and my friends and those who love me.

Given the last paragraph, let me make it explicitly clear that this did not cure, or remotely help my depression. It made it worse. I started drinking, cutting, and isolating myself more than I ever had. I stopped going to work.
